name: 5. Backend development
description: APIs, business logic, jobs, queues, caching, search, storage.

cards.subject: A resource-oriented URL
says: names a thing with a noun such as /orders/42
leaves the action to the HTTP method instead of a verb in the path
cards.use: design the address of an endpoint that fetches one order
not: puts the action in the path, as in /getOrder?id=42

cards.subject: GET
says: reads a resource without changing server state
is safe to repeat and to cache
cards.use: need to fetch data and change nothing
not: is the right method for creating a record when the body is large

cards.subject: POST
says: creates a new subordinate resource or triggers processing
is not idempotent by default, so a repeat can create a second record
cards.use: need the server to assign the id of a new record
not: is idempotent by definition

cards.subject: PUT
says: replaces the whole representation at a known URL
is idempotent, so sending it twice leaves the same end state
cards.use: need to overwrite a resource completely at an address the client already knows
not: updates only the fields that appear in the body

cards.subject: PATCH
says: applies a partial change to an existing resource
sends only the fields that should change
cards.use: need to change one field of a large resource
not: replaces the entire resource and clears omitted fields

cards.subject: DELETE
says: removes a resource
is idempotent because a repeat leaves the same end state
cards.use: need to remove a record the client can address
not: must return the deleted record in the response body

cards.subject: Statelessness
says: means each request carries everything the server needs to handle it
lets any server instance answer any request
cards.use: need to add servers behind a load balancer without sticky routing
not: requires the server to remember the previous request from each client

cards.subject: An idempotent method
says: leaves the same server state whether it is sent once or many times
makes a blind client retry safe
cards.use: must decide whether a timed-out request can be retried automatically
not: guarantees the response body is identical each time

cards.subject: CORS
says: is a browser-enforced policy that decides which other origins may read a response
is configured by the server through Access-Control headers
cards.use: need a web page on one origin to call your API on another
not: is an authentication mechanism that stops non-browser clients

cards.subject: Status 201
says: reports that a new resource was created
usually comes with a Location header pointing at the new resource
cards.use: answer a successful create request
not: is the normal reply to a read

cards.subject: Status 204
says: reports success with no response body
is a common reply to a successful DELETE
cards.use: succeed but have nothing to return
not: must carry a JSON body describing the result

cards.subject: Status 400
says: reports a request the server cannot parse or understand, such as broken JSON
blames the client rather than the server
cards.use: reject a body that is not valid JSON
not: means the server crashed while handling the request

cards.subject: Status 401
says: means the caller is not authenticated or sent invalid credentials
is normally paired with a WWW-Authenticate header
cards.use: answer a request with a missing or expired token
not: means the caller is known but lacks the role

cards.subject: Status 403
says: means the caller is identified but not permitted to do this
does not improve if the caller simply logs in again
cards.use: refuse a logged-in user who lacks the needed role
not: means the credentials were missing from the request

cards.subject: Status 404
says: reports that nothing exists at the requested URL
is sometimes returned instead of 403 so a resource's existence is not revealed
cards.use: hide that another user's record exists
not: means the server is temporarily down

cards.subject: Status 409
says: reports a conflict with the current state of the resource
fits a duplicate unique value or a stale version on update
cards.use: reject a signup whose email address is already registered
not: means the request body could not be parsed

cards.subject: Status 429
says: tells the caller it has exceeded a rate limit
is often paired with a Retry-After header
cards.use: turn away a client that is sending too many requests
not: means the server has run out of disk space

cards.subject: A consistent error shape
says: returns the same fields for every failure, such as a code and a message
lets clients handle errors with one code path
cards.use: design what every endpoint returns on failure
not: lets each endpoint invent its own error format for flexibility

cards.subject: A machine-readable error code
says: gives clients a stable identifier to branch on
stays the same even when the human message is reworded
cards.use: let a client show a specific prompt when a coupon has expired
not: is best replaced by matching on the message text

cards.subject: Hiding internal details
says: keeps stack traces and SQL text out of responses
logs the full error server-side and returns a generic message with a request id
cards.use: stop clients seeing database errors on a 500
not: helps debugging by returning the stack trace to the caller

cards.subject: Boundary validation
says: checks type, length, range and format of input at the point it enters the system
rejects bad input before any business logic runs
cards.use: want bad data stopped at the door
not: is needed only for requests from anonymous users

cards.subject: A field allowlist
says: accepts only the fields the endpoint names and ignores or rejects the rest
stops a client from setting fields it should not control
cards.use: bind a request body onto a database record safely
not: lists the fields that are forbidden and accepts everything else

cards.subject: Mass assignment
says: is a flaw where client-supplied fields are copied straight onto a model
lets a caller set fields such as isAdmin by adding them to the body
cards.use: spot why User.update(req.body) is dangerous
not: is a performance technique that updates many rows in one query

cards.subject: A parameterized query
says: sends values to the database separately from the SQL text
prevents SQL injection from user input
cards.use: build a query that includes an email typed by a user
not: is made safe by escaping quotes in a concatenated string by hand

cards.subject: A circuit breaker
says: stops calls to a failing dependency for a cooling-off period
fails fast instead of piling up slow requests
cards.use: keep a down payment provider from exhausting your threads
not: retries every failed call immediately until it works

cards.subject: Graceful degradation
says: keeps core features working when a dependency fails
serves a fallback such as a simpler result in place of the failed part
cards.use: keep a product page up while recommendations are unavailable
not: returns a 500 for the whole page if any part fails

cards.subject: A bulkhead
says: isolates resources such as thread or connection pools per dependency
stops one slow dependency from starving the others
cards.use: prevent one slow downstream from consuming every worker
not: is a cache placed in front of the database

cards.subject: Offset pagination
says: skips a number of rows and returns the next page
gets slower as the offset grows because skipped rows are still read
cards.use: build a simple page-number list over a small table
not: stays stable when rows are inserted while the client pages

cards.subject: Cursor pagination
says: continues from a marker for the last item seen
stays stable when rows are inserted or deleted during paging
cards.use: page through a feed that changes constantly
not: lets a client jump straight to page 50

cards.subject: A page size cap
says: limits how many items one request may ask for
protects the server from a client requesting everything at once
cards.use: stop limit=1000000 hurting the database
not: is unnecessary when an index exists

cards.subject: An idempotency key
says: is a client-generated unique value sent with a request
lets the server return the stored result for a repeated request instead of repeating the work
cards.use: stop a retried payment request charging twice
not: is a secret that proves who the caller is

cards.subject: A conditional GET
says: sends a validator such as If-None-Match for a cached copy
gets a 304 with no body if the resource is unchanged
cards.use: save bandwidth when a client re-requests a large unchanged document
not: always returns the full body

cards.subject: Optimistic concurrency with ETags
says: sends the version the client last saw in an If-Match header
fails the write with 412 if someone else changed the resource first
cards.use: stop two editors silently overwriting each other over HTTP
not: locks the row until the first editor finishes

cards.subject: A breaking change
says: removes, renames or changes the meaning of something clients rely on
needs a new version or a migration period
cards.use: decide whether renaming a response field is safe for existing apps
not: is limited to removing an entire endpoint

cards.subject: A backward-compatible change
says: adds something such as an optional field without altering existing behaviour
can ship without a new API version
cards.use: add a new optional field to a response
not: includes making a previously optional request field required

cards.subject: A tolerant reader
says: ignores response fields it does not recognise
lets a server add fields without breaking old clients
cards.use: write a client that survives the server adding fields
not: fails on any field it does not know

cards.subject: URL versioning
says: puts the version in the path, as in /v2/orders
makes the version visible in logs and easy to route
cards.use: run two versions of an API side by side behind a gateway
not: keeps one URL and hides the version in a custom header

cards.subject: An entry point
says: reads the request and checks who is calling
stays thin and hands the work to the business logic
cards.use: decide what a route handler should do
not: is the right place for pricing and eligibility rules

cards.subject: Business logic
says: applies the rules of the domain, such as pricing or pass marks
is written as plain modules that tests can call directly
cards.use: decide where an eligibility rule belongs
not: belongs inside the HTTP handler so it is close to the request

cards.subject: A data access layer
says: reads and writes the stored facts
hides query details from the rules that need the data
cards.use: change the database without rewriting the rules
not: decides whether a user is allowed to perform an action

cards.subject: A fat handler
says: buries validation, rules and queries in one route function
is hard to test and tends to duplicate rules across routes
cards.use: explain why the same rule has drifted apart in two endpoints
not: is the recommended way to keep logic close to the request

cards.subject: A single source of truth for a rule
says: defines a rule in one place that every caller uses
means a change is made once and tests cover it directly
cards.use: keep the page, admin tools and tests behaving the same
not: copies the rule into each caller so they stay independent

cards.subject: The repository pattern
says: puts storage behind an interface of domain-shaped methods
lets tests swap in an in-memory version
cards.use: test business rules without a real database
not: makes every query slower by adding a network hop

cards.subject: Dependency injection
says: passes a component its collaborators instead of having it create them
makes it easy to replace a real mailer with a fake in tests
cards.use: unit-test a service that sends email
not: requires a framework or container to use

cards.subject: A functional core
says: keeps decisions in pure functions with no input or output
pushes database and network calls to a thin outer shell
cards.use: make rules fast and deterministic to test
not: mixes reads and writes with the rules for simplicity

cards.subject: Authentication
says: establishes who the caller is
comes before any decision about what the caller may do
cards.use: answer who is making this request
not: decides which actions the caller may take

cards.subject: Authorization
says: decides what an identified caller may do
must be checked on every request, not only at login
cards.use: decide whether this user may edit this record
not: proves the caller's identity

cards.subject: A server-side session
says: stores an opaque session id in a cookie while the state lives on the server
can be ended immediately by deleting the server record
cards.use: need to log a user out everywhere at once
not: puts the user's data in the cookie itself

cards.subject: A JWT
says: is a signed token carrying claims such as the subject and expiry
is hard to revoke before it expires unless the server keeps extra state
cards.use: pass identity between services without a shared session store
not: hides its payload from anyone holding the token, since it is encrypted

cards.subject: Password hashing
says: uses a slow, salted one-way function such as bcrypt or Argon2
stores a result that cannot be decrypted back to the password
cards.use: store user passwords safely
not: encrypts passwords so support staff can recover them

cards.subject: Role-based access control
says: grants permissions through roles assigned to users
makes it easy to answer what an editor can do
cards.use: manage permissions for many users with a few job types
not: checks the individual record's owner

cards.subject: Object-level authorization
says: checks that this caller may access this specific record
stops a user changing the id in the URL to read someone else's data
cards.use: fix an endpoint that returns any invoice whose id is guessed
not: is satisfied once the caller has logged in

cards.subject: The principle of least privilege
says: gives each account or key only the access its job needs
limits the damage if a credential leaks
cards.use: decide what permissions a background worker's database user needs
not: gives every service the same admin rights to avoid configuration mistakes

cards.subject: CSRF
says: tricks a browser into sending an authenticated request the user did not intend
is reduced by SameSite cookies and anti-forgery tokens
cards.use: protect a cookie-authenticated form post
not: lets an attacker run scripts in the victim's page

cards.subject: An HttpOnly cookie
says: cannot be read by JavaScript running in the page
limits the damage of a cross-site scripting bug
cards.use: keep a session cookie out of reach of injected scripts
not: is sent only over encrypted connections

cards.subject: OAuth 2.0
says: delegates limited access to a resource through access tokens
is an authorization framework, not a login protocol on its own
cards.use: let a third-party app read a user's data without their password
not: proves the user's identity without any extra layer

cards.subject: A background job
says: runs outside the web request
is the right home for slow work such as sending email
cards.use: avoid making a user wait for a slow task
not: must finish before the response is sent

cards.subject: A queue
says: holds work items until a worker takes them
lets producers and workers run at different speeds
cards.use: smooth out bursts of work
not: runs the tasks itself without any worker

cards.subject: A scheduled job
says: runs on a timer such as a cron expression
suits work that must happen at set times with no request
cards.use: need to run a cleanup every night
not: is triggered only by a user action

cards.subject: An idempotent job
says: gives the same result when run twice as when run once
makes retries and duplicate deliveries harmless
cards.use: make a job safe to retry
not: is one that never fails

cards.subject: Exponential backoff with jitter
says: lengthens the wait after each failed attempt
adds randomness so many clients do not retry at the same instant
cards.use: retry a flaky service without creating a retry storm
not: retries immediately and as fast as possible

cards.subject: A dead-letter queue
says: collects messages that kept failing after the retry limit
holds them for a person to inspect instead of blocking the main queue
cards.use: deal with a message that fails every time
not: deletes failed messages to keep the queue short

cards.subject: At-least-once delivery
says: guarantees a message is delivered but may deliver it more than once
makes idempotent consumers essential
cards.use: design a consumer for a queue that can redeliver
not: guarantees each message is processed exactly once

cards.subject: A poison message
says: fails every time it is processed
blocks progress if it is retried forever without a limit
cards.use: explain why one bad message stalled a worker
not: is a message that carries a virus

cards.subject: A visibility timeout
says: hides a taken message from other workers for a set time
makes the message reappear if the worker does not acknowledge it
cards.use: explain why a slow job ran twice at the same time
not: deletes a message once it is read

cards.subject: The outbox pattern
says: writes an event row in the same transaction as the data change
lets a separate process publish the event afterwards
cards.use: avoid saving an order but losing the event, or the reverse
not: publishes the event inside the request, before the commit

cards.subject: Compute on read
says: derives a value when it is requested instead of storing it from a schedule
removes the need for a job and for keeping stored values fresh
cards.use: decide whether work needs a scheduler at all
not: is always faster than precomputing

cards.subject: Caching
says: stores the result of expensive work so it is not repeated
reuses a stored answer for later identical requests, at some cost in freshness
cards.use: avoid repeating a costly query for every request
not: always returns the newest data

cards.subject: A TTL
says: is the time after which a cached entry expires
bounds how stale a cached value can be
cards.use: decide how long data may be old
not: is the number of times an entry may be read

cards.subject: Cache invalidation
says: removes or refreshes entries when the source data changes
is the hard part of caching because stale data causes confusing bugs
cards.use: stop users seeing an old price after an edit
not: is unnecessary when a TTL is set

cards.subject: Cache-aside
says: checks the cache first and loads from the database on a miss
lets the application fill the cache and set the TTL
cards.use: add a cache without changing how writes work
not: writes to the cache and the database together on every update

cards.subject: Write-through
says: writes to the cache and the database together
keeps the cache current at the cost of slower writes
cards.use: need reads to find fresh data without waiting for a TTL
not: fills the cache only when a read misses

cards.subject: A cache stampede
says: happens when a popular entry expires and many requests rebuild it at once
is reduced by locking one rebuilder or by adding jitter to TTLs
cards.use: stop a hot key's expiry spiking the database
not: is a cache that has grown too large

cards.subject: A per-user cache key
says: includes the user in the key for personalised data
stops one user being served another user's cached response
cards.use: cache a response that contains account details
not: is safe to omit if the data is cached for a short time

cards.subject: The Cache-Control private directive
says: lets only the user's own browser store the response
stops shared caches such as a CDN keeping it
cards.use: mark a response containing account data as not for shared caches
not: lets any proxy cache the response for everyone

cards.subject: Rate limiting
says: restricts how often a caller can do something
slows password guessing and abuse
cards.use: slow down a login brute-force attack
not: makes every request faster

cards.subject: A fixed-window limiter
says: counts requests per key in a time window that then resets
can let a burst of nearly double the limit through around a window boundary
cards.use: implement a simple counter per key
not: smooths traffic exactly at all times

cards.subject: A sliding-window limiter
says: counts requests over the most recent period instead of fixed blocks
avoids the boundary burst of a fixed window
cards.use: limit requests without the boundary burst
not: resets all counters at the same moment

cards.subject: A token bucket
says: refills tokens at a steady rate and spends one per request
allows short bursts up to the bucket size
cards.use: permit bursts while holding a steady average rate
not: rejects any request that arrives faster than the average rate

cards.subject: A database index
says: lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table
speeds reads but adds cost to writes
cards.use: speed up a query that filters on one column
not: has no effect on write speed

cards.subject: The N+1 query problem
says: runs one query for a list and then one more per item
is fixed by a join or by loading the related rows in one batch
cards.use: explain why a list page makes hundreds of queries
not: is solved by adding more application servers

cards.subject: Full-text search
says: matches words in text using an index of terms
ranks results by relevance, which LIKE '%term%' cannot do
cards.use: let users search article bodies quickly
not: is the same as a LIKE '%term%' scan

cards.subject: Connection pooling
says: reuses a limited set of open database connections
stops each request paying the cost of a new connection
cards.use: avoid exhausting the database's connection limit under load
not: opens a fresh connection for every query

cards.subject: A separate search engine
says: adds ranking, typo tolerance and scale beyond the database's own features
is worth adding only when those needs appear
cards.use: decide when the database's built-in search is no longer enough
not: should be the first step for any search box

cards.subject: A database transaction
says: groups several changes into one all-or-nothing unit
can be rolled back if any step fails
cards.use: move money between two accounts
not: makes each statement independently permanent as it runs

cards.subject: Atomicity
says: means a transaction's changes all happen or none do
ensures a crash halfway leaves no partial update
cards.use: explain why half a transfer never remains
not: means concurrent transactions cannot see each other

cards.subject: Isolation
says: controls what concurrent transactions can see of each other's work
is tuned through levels that trade strictness for throughput
cards.use: decide how much concurrent transactions may interfere
not: means a transaction's changes survive a crash

cards.subject: A lost update
says: happens when two writers read the same value and the later write overwrites the earlier
is avoided with atomic updates, locks or version checks
cards.use: explain a counter that lost increments under load
not: is a row removed by a cascading delete

cards.subject: A unique constraint
says: makes the database reject duplicate values
enforces the rule even when two requests race
cards.use: stop two accounts registering the same email
not: is enforced by checking in application code before inserting

cards.subject: Optimistic locking
says: checks a version or timestamp at write time
fails the update if the row changed since it was read
cards.use: handle rare conflicts without holding locks
not: holds a row lock from read to write

cards.subject: Pessimistic locking
says: locks rows as they are read, for example with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
blocks other writers until the transaction ends
cards.use: serialise access to a hot row under heavy contention
not: never blocks another transaction

cards.subject: A deadlock
says: occurs when transactions each hold a lock the other needs
is resolved by the database aborting one transaction
cards.use: explain why two transactions froze until one was killed
not: occurs only when a table has no index

cards.subject: Eventual consistency
says: means replicas or caches converge to the same value after a delay
can show a stale read straight after a write
cards.use: explain why a read from a replica missed a fresh write
not: guarantees every read sees the latest write

cards.subject: An expand-contract migration
says: adds the new column or table first, moves code over, then removes the old one
keeps old and new code working while a deploy rolls out
cards.use: rename a column without downtime
not: drops the old column in the same deploy that adds the new one

cards.subject: Detecting type from the bytes
says: reads the file's actual content signature
ignores the type and name the client claims
cards.use: verify an upload is really a PNG
not: trusts the Content-Type header sent by the client

cards.subject: An upload size limit
says: rejects files above a fixed number of bytes
protects memory, disk and bandwidth
cards.use: stop a client uploading a huge file
not: is enforced only by the browser

cards.subject: A generated file name
says: replaces the client's name with a random or derived one
prevents collisions and path tricks in names
cards.use: store an uploaded file safely
not: keeps the original name so users can recognise it on disk

cards.subject: Storage outside the web root
says: keeps uploads where the web server does not publish them
serves them only through a route that checks permission
cards.use: stop an uploaded script being run or fetched directly
not: puts uploads in the public folder for speed

cards.subject: Path traversal
says: uses sequences such as ../ to escape the intended folder
is blocked by never joining client input into a file path
cards.use: explain how /files?name=../../secret read a private file
not: is a technique for speeding up directory listing

cards.subject: A signed URL
says: grants time-limited access to one stored object
needs no session on the storage service
cards.use: let a user download a private file directly from object storage
not: makes the file public permanently

cards.subject: Rejecting SVG uploads
says: avoids a format that can contain scripts
is a common choice for profile photo rules
cards.use: decide which image formats a photo upload may accept
not: is needed because SVG files are always too large

cards.subject: Re-encoding an uploaded image
says: decodes and writes the image again
drops metadata and embedded payloads in the original
cards.use: strip location data from uploaded photos
not: leaves the original bytes untouched

cards.subject: A log level
says: marks how serious an entry is, such as debug, info, warn or error
lets production hide noisy detail
cards.use: reduce noise in production logs
not: decides which user may read the log

cards.subject: Structured logging
says: writes entries as fields such as JSON instead of free text
makes logs searchable by user, route or request id
cards.use: filter logs by route and status
not: makes logs unreadable by machines

cards.subject: A correlation id
says: is a value attached to one request and passed through every service
lets you follow a single request across logs
cards.use: trace one failing request through several services
not: is the user's login identifier

cards.subject: Redacting secrets from logs
says: keeps passwords, tokens and API keys out of log lines
removes sensitive fields before an entry is written
cards.use: decide what to do with a request body containing a password
not: is optional because logs are private

cards.subject: A health check
says: is an endpoint a load balancer or monitor calls to see if the app is up
should answer quickly without heavy work
cards.use: let the platform restart a stuck process
not: returns the full application log

cards.subject: A readiness check
says: reports whether an instance can take traffic now, for example its database connection works
keeps a starting instance out of rotation until ready
cards.use: avoid routing traffic to an instance that cannot reach its database
not: only tells the platform that the process is alive

cards.subject: Tail latency (p99)
says: is the response time that 99 percent of requests beat
exposes slowness an average hides
cards.use: find why a few users see slow pages while the average looks fine
not: is the same as the median

cards.subject: An audit log
says: records who did what and when for sensitive actions
is append-only so history cannot be quietly rewritten
cards.use: answer who changed this user's role last week
not: is a debug log meant to be deleted often

cards.subject: A webhook
says: is an HTTP call a service makes to your endpoint when an event happens
saves the receiver from polling
cards.use: learn when a payment succeeds without polling
not: is a call your server makes to ask for new events on a timer

cards.subject: Webhook signature verification
says: recomputes an HMAC over the raw body with a shared secret
rejects calls whose signature does not match
cards.use: be sure an incoming webhook really came from the provider
not: trusts the sender's IP address alone

cards.subject: Webhook replay protection
says: rejects events whose signed timestamp is too old
stops a captured valid request being sent again later
cards.use: stop an attacker replaying a recorded webhook
not: is provided by the signature on its own

cards.subject: Acknowledging a webhook fast
says: returns a 2xx quickly and does the heavy work in a background job
avoids provider timeouts and needless redelivery
cards.use: stop a provider retrying because your handler is slow
not: processes the full event before replying

cards.subject: Deduplicating by event id
says: stores the ids of events already handled
makes redelivered webhooks harmless
cards.use: survive a provider sending the same event twice
not: assumes each event arrives exactly once

cards.subject: Configuration from the environment
says: reads settings such as keys and URLs from environment variables
keeps secrets out of the source code
cards.use: run the same build in test and production with different keys
not: hard-codes values into the repository for convenience

cards.subject: Keeping a secret out of version control
says: keeps the value out of the repository and the logs
means the credential must be rotated if it is ever pushed
cards.use: respond to an API key that was pushed to a public repository
not: is safe once the commit is deleted from the branch

cards.subject: Secret rotation
says: replaces a credential with a new one on a schedule or after exposure
works best when the system accepts old and new keys during a switch
cards.use: change a key with no downtime
not: is needed only when a developer leaves

cards.subject: A timeout on outbound calls
says: bounds how long the app waits for another service
stops a slow dependency holding workers forever
cards.use: stop a stuck partner API freezing your requests
not: is unnecessary when the partner says it is reliable

cards.subject: A fallback when a service is missing
says: keeps the product working with a simpler path when an external service is unavailable
returns a reduced result, such as keyword grading, in place of an AI call
cards.use: keep grading working when the AI provider key is absent
not: hides the failure by returning made-up results

cards.subject: Model output as untrusted input
says: is validated before use like any other external data
is never run or inserted into queries without checks
cards.use: decide how to handle text an AI model returns
not: can skip validation because the model was instructed to be safe

cards.subject: A cost budget on a paid service
says: caps spend per period for a metered API
pauses or alerts when the cap is reached
cards.use: stop a bug from running up a large bill
not: is only needed after the first invoice

cards.subject: The gglearn lib folder
says: keeps rules as plain modules such as levels.ts, grading.ts and progress.ts
gives each module one concern
cards.use: find where gglearn's business rules live
not: holds the page components

cards.subject: A gglearn level attempt
says: draws 10 questions
favours questions the learner has not yet answered correctly
passes at 80 percent
cards.use: work out how a learner passes a level
not: draws every question in the level

cards.subject: The gglearn rate limiter
says: uses a fixed window with a counter per key
keeps its counters in process memory
cards.use: understand how gglearn slows repeated attempts
not: stores counters in a shared Redis cluster

cards.subject: The gglearn limiter's memory counters
says: reset when the process restarts
are fine for one PM2 process and must move to the database if the process count changes
cards.use: scale gglearn to more than one process
not: are shared automatically between PM2 processes

cards.subject: A gglearn limiter check without a hit
says: tells whether a key is still allowed without counting a hit
lets a login be tested for blocking without using up an attempt
cards.use: ask whether a login is blocked without using up an attempt
not: always counts a hit when called

cards.subject: Clearing a gglearn limiter key
says: resets the key's counter once the action succeeds
stops a legitimate user being locked out by earlier mistakes
cards.use: handle a limiter key after a successful login
not: is only possible by restarting the process

cards.subject: The gglearn photo upload rule
says: accepts JPEG, PNG or WebP only
caps a photo at 300 KB
takes the type from the file's bytes and rejects SVG
cards.use: know what a gglearn user may upload as a photo
not: trust the file extension and accept SVG

cards.subject: The gglearn open-answer grading
says: asks Claude to judge an answer against a reference answer and rubric
falls back to a coarse keyword check when no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set
cards.use: know how gglearn marks written answers
not: marks every written answer correct when the AI is offline

cards.subject: The gglearn rival progress
says: is deterministic and calculated when read
needs no scheduler
cards.use: know how gglearn rivals advance
not: is updated every minute by a cron job

cards.subject: The gglearn finished-contest ranking
says: is computed on read
needs no stored job to produce the final table
cards.use: know how a finished gglearn contest is ranked
not: are written to the database by a nightly job

cards.subject: The ggsocial composer
says: validates each post per platform
requires a title for Reddit and caps X posts at 280 characters
cards.use: know why a draft is rejected before publishing
not: applies one limit to every platform

cards.subject: A ggsocial agent
says: does work for each brand every hour
runs as a background job
cards.use: understand how ggsocial keeps working without a user clicking
not: run only when an admin starts them

cards.subject: The ggsocial posting-time job
says: runs daily
suggests the best times to post
cards.use: find what picks posting times
not: runs on every page request

cards.subject: The ggsocial activity checklist
says: catches up every hour from facts
never overwrites a check a person recorded
cards.use: know what happens to a manually recorded check when the job runs
not: resets every item each hour regardless of who set it

cards.subject: A ggsocial workflow pause
says: stops for a person when a safety rule triggers
also stops when a score is low or a step keeps failing
cards.use: know when ggsocial hands work to a human
not: happens only when the whole system is shut down

cards.subject: The ggsocial run log
says: records what each run made
records what each run cost
cards.use: audit what a ggsocial run produced
not: keeps only error messages

cards.subject: The ggsocial AI budget
says: logs every Claude call with its cost
shows each brand's spend today
pauses a run when the brand's daily budget is spent
cards.use: know what stops AI spend running away in ggsocial
not: lets runs continue after the budget and bills later

cards.subject: The ggsocial AI reviewer
says: scores work before it goes out
stops risky items for a person whatever the settings
cards.use: know who approves risky AI-written posts
not: can be configured to approve risky items automatically

qa.q: What does this endpoint do wrong for a successful create?
qa.right: It returns 200 where 201 with a Location header would better describe creation
wrong: It uses POST for a create
It sends JSON in the body
qa.why: A create normally answers 201 and points at the new resource.

qa.q: What is the danger in this query?
qa.right: String concatenation lets a crafted email change the SQL, which is SQL injection
wrong: The query is too slow without LIMIT
SELECT * is not allowed in production
qa.why: Values must be sent as parameters, never joined into the SQL text.
qa.code: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'");

qa.q: What does this change achieve?
qa.right: The value travels separately from the SQL text, so it cannot alter the query
wrong: It encrypts the email before it is stored
It caches the query result for later
It makes the database skip the unique index
qa.why: Placeholders keep data and code apart.
qa.code: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]);

qa.q: What is missing from this handler?
qa.right: A check that the signed-in user owns this document
qa.why: Logging in is not enough; access must be checked for the specific record.

qa.q: What is the security risk in this line?
qa.right: A caller can add fields such as isAdmin to the body and set them
wrong: It deletes the user on every call
It exposes the password hash in the response
qa.why: This is mass assignment; copy only an allowlist of fields.
qa.code: await User.update(req.params.id, req.body);

qa.q: A client times out and sends this request again with the same key. What should the server do?
qa.right: Return the stored result of the first request without charging again
wrong: Charge again because the retry is a new request
Delete the first charge and create a new one
qa.why: An idempotency key lets the server detect a repeat and replay the result.

qa.q: Why is cursor pagination preferred over this for a busy feed?
qa.right: Rows inserted during paging shift offsets, causing repeats or skips, and large offsets are slow
wrong: Cursors return more rows per request
LIMIT is slower than a cursor
qa.why: A cursor continues from the last seen item, so inserts do not move the page.
qa.code: SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

qa.q: A client sends this request and the resource has not changed. What does the server return?
qa.right: 304 Not Modified with no body
qa.why: If-None-Match with a matching ETag means the cached copy is current.
qa.code:
GET /report/9
If-None-Match: "v42"

qa.q: A client updates with this header but another user changed the record first. What status fits?
qa.right: 412 Precondition Failed
qa.why: If-Match makes the write conditional on the version the client saw.
qa.code:
PUT /notes/5
If-Match: "v7"

qa.q: What is wrong with this loop?
qa.right: It runs one query per order, the N+1 problem
wrong: It makes the query too fast
qa.why: Load customers in one batch or use a join.

qa.q: What happens if the second statement fails and the code runs ROLLBACK?
qa.right: Neither balance changes
qa.why: A transaction is all-or-nothing.

qa.q: Which version avoids a lost update under concurrent withdrawals?
qa.right: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 10
wrong: Read the balance in code, subtract 10, then write the result back
Read the balance twice before writing
Add a sleep between the read and the write
qa.why: A single atomic statement checks and changes together.
qa.code: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 10;

qa.q: Why must the HMAC be computed over the raw request body?
qa.right: Re-serialised JSON can differ byte for byte from what the sender signed
qa.why: Verification must use exactly the bytes that were signed.
qa.code: const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(rawBody).digest("hex");

qa.q: Which pattern is this?
qa.right: Cache-aside
qa.why: The application checks the cache, loads on a miss and fills the cache.

qa.q: What is the purpose of Math.random() in this delay?
qa.right: Jitter, so many clients do not retry at the same moment
wrong: It makes the delay shorter than the base
It stops the retry count rising
qa.why: Randomised delays spread out retries.
qa.code: const delay = Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt) * Math.random();

qa.q: What is a weakness of this limiter?
qa.right: A burst around the window boundary can pass nearly double the limit
qa.why: Fixed windows reset all at once, so two bursts straddling the edge both pass.

qa.q: What does this header allow?
qa.right: Only the user's own browser may store the response, for 60 seconds
wrong: Any CDN may store it for 60 minutes
It is cached forever by shared proxies
qa.why: private excludes shared caches.
qa.code: Cache-Control: private, max-age=60

qa.q: Why can a client not simply edit the role in this token?
qa.right: The signature would no longer match, so the server rejects it
wrong: Roles are ignored by the server
The token is stored on the server
qa.why: A JWT is signed, so tampering is detected, though the payload is readable.

qa.q: What is the risk in this code?
qa.right: A name such as ../../etc/passwd escapes the uploads folder
wrong: The file is read too slowly
qa.why: Never join client input into a path; use generated names.
qa.code: fs.readFile("/uploads/" + req.query.name);

qa.q: What is the benefit of logging in this form?
qa.right: Fields can be searched and filtered by route, user or request id
qa.why: Structured entries are machine-readable.
qa.code: logger.info({ requestId, userId, route, ms: 84 }, "request done");

qa.q: What is wrong with this log call?
qa.right: It writes a password into the logs
qa.why: Secrets must never be logged.
qa.code: logger.error("login failed", { email, password });

qa.q: Why would a readiness endpoint return 503 here?
qa.right: The instance cannot reach its database, so traffic should be kept away
wrong: The disk is full of logs
The user is not logged in
qa.why: Readiness tells the load balancer whether to route traffic.
qa.code: GET /ready  ->  503 { "db": "unreachable" }

qa.q: What can happen if the worker crashes right after send()?
qa.right: The message is redelivered and the email goes out twice
wrong: The message moves to a database table
qa.why: At-least-once delivery means work must be idempotent.

qa.q: What problem does this pattern solve?
qa.right: The data change and its event are saved together, so neither can be lost alone
wrong: It removes the need for transactions
qa.why: The outbox row commits with the order and is published later.

qa.q: What does this statement do on a redelivered webhook?
qa.right: Ignores the duplicate event because its id is already stored
wrong: Raises an error and stops the server
qa.why: A unique event id makes handling idempotent.
qa.code:
INSERT INTO events (event_id, body) VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING;

qa.q: Which query does this index help most?
qa.right: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 5 ORDER BY created_at DESC
wrong: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id
qa.why: A composite index on (user_id, created_at) serves both filter and order.
qa.code: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders (user_id, created_at);

qa.q: What should a well-behaved client do after this response?
qa.right: Wait about 30 seconds before trying again
wrong: Treat the request as permanently failed
qa.why: Retry-After says when to retry.
qa.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30

qa.q: What does the 12 control here?
qa.right: The cost factor, making each hash slower and brute force harder
qa.why: Higher cost slows every guess.
qa.code: const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12);

qa.q: What does HttpOnly do in this cookie?
qa.right: Stops page JavaScript reading the cookie
qa.why: HttpOnly limits the damage of cross-site scripting.
qa.code: Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

qa.q: What does the layering in this handler break?
qa.right: The pricing rule sits in the handler, so other callers and tests cannot reuse it
qa.why: Move the rule to a business-logic module and call it from the handler.

qa.q: A learner answers 8 of 10 questions correctly on a gglearn level. What happens?
qa.right: The attempt passes, because 80 percent is the pass mark
wrong: It fails, since 9 of 10 is needed
It passes only after a second attempt
It is graded by Claude before counting
qa.why: The company rule is 10 questions with an 80 percent pass mark.

qa.q: gglearn runs a second PM2 process. What happens to its rate limit counters?
qa.right: Each process keeps its own counters, so the effective limit grows until counters move to the database
qa.why: Counters live in process memory.

qa.q: A user uploads a file named photo.png whose bytes are an SVG. What do gglearn's photo rules do?
qa.right: Reject it, because the type comes from the bytes and SVG is not allowed
wrong: Accept it because of the .png name
Accept it and convert it to JPEG
Accept it after reducing it to 300 KB
qa.why: Type is read from content, not the name.

qa.q: ggsocial is composing a post for X with 320 characters. What happens?
qa.right: The composer's per-platform validation rejects it because of the 280 character cap
wrong: It posts and X trims it
It is split into two automatically
It is accepted if a title is added
qa.why: X is capped at 280 characters.

qa.q: A brand's daily AI budget in ggsocial is spent while a run is in progress. What happens?
qa.right: The run is paused
wrong: The run continues and bills later
qa.why: ggsocial pauses a run when the brand's daily AI budget is spent.

qa.q: There is no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY on the server. How does gglearn grade a written answer?
qa.right: With a coarse keyword fallback so the product still works
wrong: It refuses to show the question
It waits until a key appears
qa.why: The fallback keeps grading available.

qa.q: A person recorded a check on the ggsocial activity checklist and the hourly job runs. What happens to that check?
qa.right: It stays as recorded; the job never overwrites it
wrong: It is reset to the job's value
qa.why: Manual checks win over the job.

qa.q: A dependency is slow and every worker retries instantly, making it worse. What do you add first?
qa.right: Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry limit
wrong: A longer timeout with no retry limit
Retry faster so it recovers sooner
qa.why: Spreading and limiting retries lets the dependency recover.

qa.q: A customer was charged twice after a mobile app lost signal and retried. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Send an idempotency key and have the server store the result
qa.why: The key makes the retry safe.

qa.q: Users report seeing another person's account page after a CDN was added. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: A personalised response was cached in a shared cache without a per-user key
wrong: The password hashing cost is too low
The session cookie is too short
qa.why: Mark private data private or key the cache by user.

qa.q: A password-reset endpoint is being used to flood users with email. What do you do first?
qa.right: Rate limit by account and by IP and return the same reply whether or not the account exists
qa.why: Throttling and uniform replies reduce abuse and account probing.

qa.q: One malformed message makes a worker fail repeatedly and blocks the queue. What should happen?
qa.right: After a retry limit, move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection
qa.why: A dead-letter queue unblocks the main queue.

qa.q: Mobile apps in the wild depend on a field called total. The team wants to rename it. What is safest?
qa.right: Add the new field, keep the old one, announce a deprecation and remove it later
wrong: Rename it now and update the web app only
Rename it and bump the patch number
Remove the field and return null
qa.why: Renaming is a breaking change; overlap lets clients migrate.

qa.q: Two admins edit the same record and one silently overwrites the other. What is the best fix?
qa.right: Add a version check so the second write fails with a conflict
qa.why: Optimistic concurrency detects the conflict.

qa.q: A webhook provider keeps retrying because your handler takes 40 seconds. What do you change?
qa.right: Verify the signature, store the event, return 2xx and process in a background job
wrong: Drop all events during peak hours
qa.why: Acknowledge fast, work later, dedupe by event id.

qa.q: A deploy drops a column while old instances still read it. Which approach avoids the outage?
qa.right: Expand-contract: stop using the column in code first, then drop it later
wrong: Lock the whole table until deploy ends
qa.why: Migrations must work with old and new code during rollout.

qa.q: An upload endpoint is receiving multi-gigabyte files. What is the right defence?
qa.right: Enforce a size limit early and stream rather than buffering in memory
wrong: Rely on the browser to stop it
qa.why: Limits protect memory and bandwidth.

qa.q: A popular cache key expires and the database spikes as many requests rebuild it. What helps?
qa.right: Let one request rebuild while others wait, and add jitter to TTLs
qa.why: This is a cache stampede.

qa.q: Users see SQL errors and stack traces in 500 responses. What is the right fix?
qa.right: Log full detail server-side and return a generic message with a request id
qa.why: Errors should not leak internals.

qa.q: A secret key was pushed to a repository. What is the first step?
qa.right: Rotate the key, then clean up and review access
wrong: Delete the commit and carry on
Wait to see if it is used
qa.why: A pushed secret must be treated as exposed.

qa.q: Searching with LIKE '%term%' is slow on a large table. What is the next step?
qa.right: Use the database's full-text search with an index, and add a search engine only if needed
qa.why: Full-text indexes avoid scanning every row.

qa.q: Average latency looks fine but some users complain of slowness. What do you check?
qa.right: Tail latency such as p95 and p99
qa.why: Averages hide slow outliers.

qa.q: An endpoint returns another user's invoice when the id in the URL is changed. What is the fix?
qa.right: Check on the server that the invoice belongs to the caller
qa.why: Object-level authorization is the missing control.

qa.q: A report takes 40 seconds and times out requests. What is a good design?
qa.right: Accept the request, return 202 with a status location, and run it as a background job
wrong: Run it on every page load
qa.why: Slow work belongs outside the request.

qa.q: A payment provider outage is taking down your whole checkout. What do you add?
qa.right: A timeout, a circuit breaker and a fallback path
qa.why: Fail fast and degrade gracefully.

qa.q: An AI model's reply is placed straight into an SQL string. What is the right approach?
qa.right: Treat it as untrusted input: validate it and use parameters
wrong: Trust it because it is generated
qa.why: Model output is external data.

qa.q: Which is the better division of work?
qa.right: The handler checks the caller and calls a business module that applies the rules
wrong: The handler contains the rules and the queries
The database client makes authorization decisions
The browser applies the discount rules
qa.why: Thin entry points and shared rule modules.

qa.q: A signup with an existing email should respond with which status?
qa.right: 409 Conflict
qa.why: The request conflicts with current state.

qa.q: Which HTTP method fits reading a list without side effects?
qa.right: GET
qa.why: GET is safe and cacheable.

qa.q: Which pair describes 401 versus 403?
qa.right: 401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but not allowed
wrong: 401 means server error; 403 means rate limited
qa.why: The distinction is identity versus permission.
